title: High-Field EPR/ENDOR of N/Be Centers for Defect Engineering in 6H-SiC
authors: Yuliya Ermakova, Ekaterina Dmitrieva, Margarita Sadovnikova, Fadis Murzakhanov, George Mamin, Sergey Nagalyuk, Evgeny Mokhov, Marat Gafurov
abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC) in its various structural modifications is widely used in power semiconductor electronics, operating under extreme conditions of high temperature, high voltage, and intense radiation. The discovery of spin defects (S>0) with unique optical and coherent properties has further positioned SiC as a promising platform for quantum technologies. Here, we investigate a 6H-SiC single crystal co-doped with nitrogen and beryllium at concentrations of 1018 cm-3, using continuous-wave and pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and electron-nuclear double resonance (ENDOR). To enhance spectral resolution, experiments were conducted in the W-band (94 GHz; B = 3.4 T). Pulsed EPR identified nitrogen donors and beryllium acceptors in various lattice positions, allowing for the determination of their phase coherence and spin-lattice relaxation times. ENDOR measurements elucidated the electron-nuclear interactions with the local silicon and carbon environment, including distant coordination spheres. The observed hyperfine structures indicated highly delocalized spin density within the supercell. The TRIPLE resonance spectra verify coupled nuclear spin subspaces from different coordination spheres due to defect spin density. These results demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating dual impurities with distinct functional roles while preserving the crystal lattice`s structural features.
summary: The research uses high-field EPR/ENDOR spectroscopy to investigate nitrogen (N) donor and beryllium (Be) acceptor impurities co-doped into 6H-SiC. By measuring detailed spin interactions, the authors differentiate the electronic properties of these two types of defects. This work is vital for defect engineering, showing how N centers are suitable for quantum memory while Be centers provide sensitive local strain measurements.
main_problem: To characterize co-doped impurities (Nitrogen donor and Beryllium acceptor) in 6H-SiC to understand defect engineering for quantum technologies.
main_result: The study successfully differentiated the electronic and nuclear properties of N and Be centers, showing that N donors are stable for quantum memory while Be acceptors act as sensitive probes of local lattice strain via large quadrupole splittings.
method: High-field Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) and Electron–Nuclear Double Resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy were employed to probe spin interactions at high spectral resolution.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 6H-SiC single crystal co-doped with N donors and Be acceptors. The analysis utilizes models incorporating hyperfine and quadrupole interactions, often described by an axial spin Hamiltonian for the electronic spin centers.
key_observables: Hyperfine coupling constants (A), nuclear quadrupole splitting (Q), electron spin relaxation times ($T_1$, $T_2$), and spectral line patterns (quartets).
important_parameters: Doping concentrations ($\sim 10^{18} 	ext{ cm}^{-3}$); W-band frequency ($94 	ext{ GHz}$); Temperature regimes (low temperature for high resolution).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed spectral features can be mapped to specific defect sites and local environments, allowing for quantitative extraction of interaction parameters.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure showing N and Be impurities in different lattice configurations, and show W-band ENDOR spectra demonstrating TRIPLE resonance effects.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need to characterize co-doped defects; it then details the use of high-field EPR/ENDOR techniques to measure spectroscopic signatures (hyperfine structure, relaxation times) for both N and Be centers; finally, it compares these findings to elucidate distinct functional roles for each impurity type.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses solid-state quantum hardware by characterizing spin defects in a wide-bandgap semiconductor. The detailed measurement of hyperfine and quadrupole interactions provides crucial input parameters for modeling defect qubits and understanding environmental decoherence mechanisms.
